notes.definition: An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements, usually other metals or carbon. Most metals in everyday use are alloys, including bronze, brass, gold jewellery alloys, steels and aluminium alloys, because alloys have more useful properties than the pure metals.
explanation: Most metals in everyday use are alloys. Pure metals are often too soft for many uses because their atoms are arranged in regular layers that can slide over each other easily. In an alloy, atoms of different sizes distort the layers, making it more difficult for them to slide, so alloys are harder and stronger than the pure metals. Alloys can also be designed to resist corrosion or to have a low density.

Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin. It is harder than copper and resists corrosion, so it is used for statues, medals, bells and ship propellers. Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. It is hard, does not corrode easily and has an attractive gold colour, so it is used for musical instruments, door handles, keys and plumbing fittings.

Gold used as jewellery is usually an alloy with silver, copper and zinc, because pure gold is too soft and would bend and wear away. The proportion of gold in the alloy is measured in carats, with 24 carat being 100% (pure) gold. So 18 carat gold is 18/24 = 75% gold, and 9 carat gold is 9/24 = 37.5% gold. Percentage of gold = (carats ÷ 24) × 100. Lower carat gold is harder and cheaper, but less valuable.

Steels are alloys of iron that contain specific amounts of carbon and other metals. High carbon steel is strong but brittle, so it is used for cutting tools and hammers. Low carbon steel is softer and more easily shaped, so it is used for car body panels, wire and food cans. Steels containing chromium and nickel (stainless steels) are hard and resistant to corrosion, so they are used for cutlery, sinks, saucepans and surgical instruments.

Aluminium alloys are low density (light) and strong, so they are used in aircraft, bicycle frames and high-speed trains. You should be able to recall a use of each named alloy and interpret and evaluate data on the composition and properties of alloys to explain why a particular alloy is chosen for a particular use.
keyFacts: Most metals in everyday use are alloys.
Bronze = copper + tin. Brass = copper + zinc.
Gold jewellery is usually an alloy of gold with silver, copper and zinc.
Gold purity is measured in carats: 24 carat = 100% gold; 18 carat = 75% gold.
Steels are alloys of iron with specific amounts of carbon and other metals.
High carbon steel: strong but brittle. Low carbon steel: softer and more easily shaped.
Stainless steel contains chromium and nickel: hard and resistant to corrosion.
Alloys are harder because different-sized atoms distort the layers so they cannot slide easily.

keyTerms.definition: A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements, usually metals or carbon.
An alloy of copper and tin.
An alloy of copper and zinc.
A measure of the proportion of gold in an alloy; 24 carat is 100% gold.
An alloy of iron containing specific amounts of carbon and other metals.
A steel containing chromium and nickel that is hard and resistant to corrosion.
Breaks or shatters easily rather than bending.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think 18 carat gold is 18% gold.
misconceptions.right: In fact carats are out of 24, so 18 carat gold is 18 ÷ 24 × 100 = 75% gold.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think alloys are compounds.
misconceptions.right: In fact alloys are mixtures; the elements are not chemically bonded in fixed proportions.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think steel is a pure metal.
misconceptions.right: In fact steel is an alloy of iron with carbon and often other metals.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think high carbon steel is better in every way because it is stronger.
misconceptions.right: In fact high carbon steel is brittle; low carbon steel is softer and more easily shaped, which is better for car bodies and cans.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often mix up bronze and brass.
misconceptions.right: In fact bronze is copper and tin; brass is copper and zinc.

realWorld: Saxophones and trumpets are made of brass because it is easily shaped, resists corrosion and looks attractive.
Stainless steel (iron with chromium and nickel) is used for cutlery and surgical instruments because it does not corrode.
Aircraft bodies are made from aluminium alloys because they are strong but have low density.
Olympic 'bronze' medals and many statues are made from bronze.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is for separate Chemistry (8462) only.
Bronze (copper and tin), brass (copper and zinc), gold alloys (with silver, copper and zinc) and their uses.
Steels: high carbon steel (strong but brittle), low carbon steel (softer, easily shaped), stainless steel (chromium and nickel: hard, corrosion resistant). Aluminium alloys are low density.
examTips: Learn the pairs exactly: bronze = copper + tin, brass = copper + zinc. Mixing them up is a common way to lose marks.
For carat questions, always divide by 24, not 100.
When asked why an alloy is used, link a property to the use, for example stainless steel resists corrosion, so it is used for cutlery.
To explain hardness, describe the structure: different-sized atoms distort the layers, so they cannot slide over each other as easily.
Use data in the question: compare densities, strength or corrosion resistance to justify a choice.
summary: Bronze: copper and tin. Brass: copper and zinc.
Gold jewellery: gold alloyed with silver, copper and zinc; 24 carat = 100% gold.
Steels: iron with carbon and other metals; high carbon (strong, brittle), low carbon (easily shaped).
Stainless steel (chromium and nickel) is hard and corrosion resistant.

questions.question: Bronze is an alloy of copper and which other metal?
markScheme: 1 mark: Tin
questions.explanation: Bronze is copper and tin. Copper and zinc make brass.

questions.question: Brass is an alloy of copper and which other metal?
markScheme: 1 mark: Zinc
questions.explanation: Brass is copper and zinc; bronze is copper and tin.

questions.question: What percentage of gold is in 24 carat gold?
markScheme: 1 mark: 100%
questions.explanation: 24 carat is pure gold. Carats are out of 24, not out of 100.

questions.question: Which metals are added to iron to make stainless steel?
markScheme: 1 mark: chromium and nickel
questions.explanation: Chromium and nickel make stainless steel hard and resistant to corrosion.

questions.question: Which steel would be best for making car body panels?
options: High carbon steel, because it is brittle
Stainless steel, because it is the cheapest
Low carbon steel, because it is softer and more easily shaped
Pure iron, because it is hardest
markScheme: 1 mark: low carbon steel, softer and easily shaped
questions.explanation: Car panels are pressed into shape, so a soft, easily shaped steel is needed. Pure iron is soft, not hard.

questions.question: Why is pure gold rarely used for jewellery?
options: It is too soft and wears away easily
markScheme: 1 mark: it is too soft
questions.explanation: Gold is very soft, so it is alloyed with silver, copper and zinc to make it harder. Gold does not corrode.

questions.question: Which property makes aluminium alloys suitable for aircraft?
markScheme: 1 mark: low density
questions.explanation: Aircraft need light but strong materials, so low density aluminium alloys are used.

questions.question: A jeweller has 9, 14, 18 and 22 carat gold. Which would make the hardest-wearing ring?
markScheme: 1 mark: 9 carat
questions.explanation: 9 carat has the lowest proportion of soft gold and the most of the other metals, so it is the hardest, although least valuable.

questions.question: Which is a typical use of high carbon steel?
markScheme: 1 mark: cutting tools
questions.explanation: High carbon steel is strong and hard (but brittle), suitable for cutting tools. The other uses need easily shaped low carbon steel.

questions.question:
Pure gold is 24 carat.
Calculate the percentage of gold in 18 carat gold.
markScheme: 1 mark: 75%
questions.explanation: Carats are out of 24: 18 ÷ 24 = 0.75 = 75%.

questions.question:
Pure gold is 24 carat.
Calculate the percentage of gold in 22 carat gold.
Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
questions.explanation: 22 ÷ 24 × 100 = 91.666...% = 91.7% to 3 significant figures.

A jeweller melts a ring together with some pure gold to make a new alloy.

Calculate the carat value of the new alloy.
markScheme: 1 mark: gold in ring = 0.75 × 6.0 = 4.5 g
1 mark: total gold = 7.5 g in 9.0 g of alloy
questions.explanation: Fraction of gold = 7.5 ÷ 9.0 = 0.8333, × 24 = 20 carat.

questions.question: Give one use of bronze.
markScheme: 1 mark: statues / medals / bells / ship propellers
questions.explanation: Bronze is hard and resists corrosion.

questions.question: Give one use of brass.
markScheme: 1 mark: musical instruments / door handles / keys / plumbing fittings
questions.explanation: Brass is hard, resists corrosion and has an attractive gold colour.

questions.question: State what is meant by an alloy and give the main metal in steel.

questions.question: Name two metals that are mixed with gold to make jewellery alloys.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: silver / copper / zinc
questions.explanation: The specification states gold jewellery is usually an alloy with silver, copper and zinc.

questions.question:
Table 1 gives data for four materials.
A company is choosing a material for the frame of a racing bicycle, and another material for kitchen sinks.
Evaluate the materials for each use.
Recommend the best material for each use.
markScheme: Indicative content: bicycle frame needs low density, high strength and corrosion resistance; aluminium alloy has the lowest density (2.8 g/cm³, about one third of steel) with high strength and good corrosion resistance, so best for racing bike; stainless steel is very strong but nearly three times as dense; low carbon steel rusts and is heavy; brass is densest and only medium strength. Kitchen sinks need very good corrosion resistance (in contact with water), hardness; density less important; stainless steel best (chromium and nickel make it hard and corrosion resistant); low carbon steel would rust; brass more expensive and denser; aluminium alloy possible but less hard.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): uses data to compare all relevant materials for both uses, links properties to uses and gives justified recommendations.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): makes a recommendation for both uses with some use of data.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): makes a recommendation for one use with a simple reason.
questions.explanation: Pick out the property that matters most for each use, then quote and compare the data.

questions.question: Describe the composition and one use of each of these alloys: bronze, brass, stainless steel and an aluminium alloy, giving a property that makes it suitable for that use.
markScheme: Indicative content: bronze, copper and tin, statues or bells, hard and resists corrosion; brass, copper and zinc, musical instruments or door handles, hard, attractive, does not corrode; stainless steel, iron with chromium and nickel (and carbon), cutlery or sinks, hard and resistant to corrosion; aluminium alloy, aircraft, low density and strong.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct composition and a use with linked property for at least three alloys.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): correct composition or use for one or two alloys.
questions.explanation: Each answer should link the property to the use.

questions.question: Suggest why a 9 carat gold ring is cheaper than an 18 carat gold ring of the same mass.
markScheme: 1 mark: 9 carat contains less gold (37.5% compared with 75%, half as much)
1 mark: gold is more expensive than the silver, copper and zinc that replace it
questions.explanation: The price depends mainly on the mass of gold present.

questions.question: Which statement about most metals in everyday use is correct?
markScheme: 1 mark: they are alloys
questions.explanation: Pure metals are often too soft, so most everyday metals are alloys.
